name: Northern Rengma / Ntenyi, Mills 1937 'language B'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mills, J. P. 1937. The Rengma Nagas. London: Macmillan & Co. Part VI 'Language', pp. 285-309 (A = Southern/Western Rengma [nre], B = Northern Rengma/Ntenyi [nnl], C = Eastern Rengma/Meluri [npo]). Archive.org DLI scan dli.csl.3979.
catalog_locator: p. 290 fn. 1; context p. 285 (B = 'the language of the Northern group' of Western Rengmas, standard = upper khels of Tesophenyu) and p. 287 (spelling key, tones noted only where of special importance)
catalog_quote: In B “ bad ” = mehe with the final e low, and “ good ” = mehe with the final e high—an excellent example of the great importance of tone in the language. [p. 290 fn. 1] ... No one but a specialist can ever hope adequately to analyse a Naga language, with its tones, its rich vocabulary and its nuances of meaning that are so hard to grasp. [p. 285] ... I have used no diacritical marks, and tones have only been noted where of special importance. Only syllables which are very strongly long or short have been so marked. [p. 287]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.locator: p. 290 fn. 1 (PDF page 334 of the DLI scan); context p. 285 defines B as 'the language of the Northern group' of Western Rengmas, standard = upper khels of Tesophenyu
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (428 pp., text present) with extracted text. PDF page 334 carries the printed header "290 THE RENGMA NAGAS PART" and the footnote reads exactly: "1 In B “ bad ” = mehe with the final e low, and “ good ” = mehe with the final e high—an excellent example of the great importance of tone in the language." the compiler quote matches word for word (only straight vs curly quotation marks differ). The footnote is anchored to "n ’tsii mehe 1 (B)" in the Case paragraph on the same page. I re-read pp. 285-288 (PDF 329-332): p. 285 defines B as "the language of the Northern group" of Western Rengmas, spoken in the upper khels of Tesophenyu, Kotsenyu, Kotsenishinyu and Kitagha, standard = upper T…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement on Northern Rengma prosody says the language is tonal (a lexical tone minimal pair on the final syllable); nothing is said anywhere about word stress or accent placement. Mills adds (pp. 286-287) that tones are noted only where of special importance and that only very strongly long or short syllables are marked.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source is a 1937 ethnographer's outline, not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (citation forms in a comparative wordlist of three Rengma languages). Mills p. 287 also notes only syllable length 'where very strongly long or short'; the later Namkung 1996 inventory (from Marrison 1967) records neither tone nor stress for Ntenyi.
new_statements.identity_note: Northern Rengma (nort2725, ISO nnl) = Ntenyi/Nthenyi = Mills 1937's 'language B' (Northern group of the Western Rengmas; standard = upper khels of Tesophenyu, also Kotsenyu, Kotsenishinyu, Kitagha). It is a different language from Rengma proper / Southern Rengma (sout2732, nre; Mills' A, Nzang/Nzon khwen, Tseminyu and Karbi Anglong dialects), which is the language described by Debnath 2023, Longmailai 2019 and Rengma & Kumar 1973, and from Meluri/Pochuri (Mills' C). Namkung 1996's 'Ntenyi' entry and Marrison 1967's Ntenyi chapter are both built on Mills' B wordlists.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Only a brief spelling key (p. 286-287: 'I have used no diacritical marks, and tones have only been noted where of special importance') and a footnote on p. 290 giving a tonal minimal pair in B ('bad' vs 'good' = mehe, final e low vs high) as 'an excellent example of the great importance of tone in the language'; a few vocabulary items later marked 'on a high/low note'.

sources.citation: Debnath, Rupak. 2023. A Phonological description of Nzang Terüpvunyu khwen (Assam Rengma). Self-archived (archive.org / academia.edu).
sources.note: Describes Rengma proper (nre / sout2732), not Northern Rengma: three level tonemes (low, mid, high) in both Terüpvunyu and Tseminyu dialects, prefixes copy root tone; the word 'stress' does not occur. Not applicable to nort2725 except as a statement that the sister language is tonal.

sources.citation: Debnath, Rupak. 2023. Rengma Dialects (short self-archived note; comparative 32-item wordlist of Nzang/Nzon khwen, Nthenyi [from Semy 2016] and Meluri [from Mills 1937]).
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone; establishes that Nthenyi (Northern Rengma = Mills' Rengma B) and Rengma proper are different languages and cites Semy 2016 Northern Rengma Dictionary as the Nthenyi data source.

sources.citation: Coupe, Alexander R. 2012. Overcounting numeral systems and their relevance to sub-grouping in the Tibeto-Burman languages of Nagaland. Language and Linguistics 13(1): 193-220.
sources.note: Glottolog's subclassification source for nort2725; may contain transcribed Ntenyi numerals with tone marks from Coupe's own fieldwork, indicating whether the language is analysed as tonal by a modern phonologist.

sources.note: No descriptive reference for the language beyond Marrison 1967 (phd, 300+460 pp., lists Northern and Southern Rengma among 31 languages) and Namkung 1996.

sources.citation: Namkung, Ju (ed.). 1996. Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages. STEDT Monograph 3. Berkeley: Center for Southeast Asia Studies. Entry NTENYI, pp. 304-305 (data source Marrison 1967 pp. 362-363, whose lexical data come from Mills 1937).
sources.note: Segment inventory and syllable canon (N)(C)V(N) only; no tone and no stress information for Ntenyi. The RENGMA entry pp. 338-339 (Rengma proper, nre) is likewise segments only.
